strengths: Addresses an important gap: systematic evaluation of MLLM abilities in assessing visualization quality and aesthetics, a domain-specific challenge that has been underexplored

Comprehensive and rigorously constructed benchmark: 3,090 expert-annotated samples with detailed three-stage annotation pipeline, quality control mechanisms, and explicit screening criteria for annotators

Theoretically grounded evaluation framework: Fidelity, Expressiveness, and Aesthetics framework draws from established design principles and is operationalized into 6 measurable, orthogonal dimensions

Thorough empirical analysis revealing systematic model biases: identifies score inflation, overly conservative behavior, and performance degradation with visualization complexity; provides insights about different 'evaluation personalities' across models

Clear presentation and extensive documentation: Well-organized figures, detailed case studies, comprehensive appendices supporting reproducibility with dataset statistics, implementation details, and evaluation criteria

Demonstrates statistically significant improvements: VisJudge achieves 19.8% MAE reduction and 58.7% correlation improvement over GPT-5, with domain-specific fine-tuning showing practical effectiveness
Valuable resource for community: Benchmark and trained model provide infrastructure for future research on MLLM capabilities in specialized evaluation tasks
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Core contribution is primarily a benchmark dataset and evaluation framework rather than novel algorithms, architectures, or theoretical insights; fine-tuning uses standard techniques (LoRA, GRPO)

Insufficient analysis of failure mechanisms: Identifies that models fail and exhibit systematic biases but provides limited mechanistic understanding of why; missing investigation into which architectural or training decisions lead to poor performance
Framework validation incomplete: Lacks ablation studies validating the necessity and sufficiency of the 6 dimensions; no comparison with alternative decompositions of visualization quality

Statistical rigor could be strengthened: Reported improvements lack formal significance testing, confidence intervals, or bootstrapped error estimates; claims of superiority would benefit from hypothesis testing

Generalization concerns: Annotator demographics concentrated in English-speaking regions; web-crawled visualizations may over-represent business/data journalism types; limited discussion of domain transferability to scientific or specialized visualization types

Incomplete comparison with related work: Mentions existing benchmarks (VisEval, VIS-Shepherd) but lacks quantitative comparison of coverage, annotation quality, and comprehensiveness; limited discussion of alternative evaluation frameworks

Limited practical application guidance: Unclear how practitioners would deploy the trained model in real-world scenarios; missing discussion of integration with visualization tools or deployment considerations

Potential reproducibility questions: While details are extensive, explicit statements about dataset public availability, access terms, and licensing are unclear; full prompt specifications for GPT-4 experiments may not be fully reproducible

strengths: Rigorous and well-documented dataset construction with 3,090 expert-annotated samples across diverse visualization types and multiple annotation stages (initial → quality control → expert validation)
Theoretically grounded evaluation framework based on established visualization design principles (Fidelity, Expressiveness, Aesthetics) with clear operationalization into measurable sub-dimensions
Comprehensive empirical evaluation of multiple representative MLLMs with systematic bias analysis (score inflation, conservative behavior) and detailed case studies illustrating model failure modes
Extensive transparency with detailed appendices documenting evaluation criteria, annotation procedures, implementation details, and commitment to release benchmark and model
Large scale (3,090 samples) and broad coverage (32 chart types, single/multiple visualizations, dashboards) providing meaningful evaluation scope
weaknesses: Severely limited technical novelty: VisJudge is merely a straightforward fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B model using standard RL with composite reward function—no novel architecture, methodology, or algorithmic contribution

Fundamental benchmark validity concerns: relies entirely on subjective human judgment without user studies, downstream task validation, or evidence that high-scoring visualizations are actually more useful for end users in practice

Problematic model generalization: training and test data from same distribution (VisJudge-Bench), no cross-dataset validation, and only three expert judges for subjective aesthetic dimensions; potential bias from using GPT-4o for adaptive question generation
Incomplete baselines: no comparison against other visualization quality evaluation methods, heuristic approaches, or ablation studies on VisJudge training components

Unclear practical utility: no demonstration of real-world integration with visualization tools, no evidence that automated scoring improves design outcomes, practitioners may prefer established guidelines or user feedback

Limited generalization scope: primarily English visualizations with unclear multilingual generalization, web-sourced data may not represent domain-specific uses, findings specific to current-generation MLLMs
Insufficient statistical rigor: no significance testing between model performance differences, annotation quality control depends on subjective judgment for inherently subjective aesthetic dimensions

strengths: Novel and timely contribution - first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating MLLMs' visualization quality assessment capabilities, addressing a genuine research gap
Rigorous three-stage dataset construction with 3,090 expert-annotated samples, systematic quality control mechanisms, and 84% cross-validation rate demonstrating robustness
Well-grounded evaluation framework based on classical 'Fidelity, Expressiveness, and Aesthetics' principles with operationalized sub-dimensions and context-aware scoring criteria

Comprehensive experimental evaluation of 7 representative MLLMs with systematic analysis of model biases and their correction through domain-specific fine-tuning (19.8% MAE reduction, 58.7% correlation improvement)
Thorough documentation with extensive appendices enabling reproducibility and practical use of the benchmark and evaluation framework
Clear demonstration of practical impact - VisJudge achieves significant improvements over general-purpose MLLMs and established baselines
Methodological rigor including systematic bias identification and analysis across visualization complexity levels, types, and quality ranges
weaknesses: Limited scope - focuses exclusively on static 2D visualizations, excluding interactive, animated, 3D, and emerging visualization types that represent modern practices
Insufficient analysis of dimension relationships - no ablation studies showing which of the six evaluation dimensions contribute most to quality assessment or analysis of potential redundancies

Data collection methodology concerns - keyword-based web crawling may introduce systematic biases; limited discussion of style evolution, cultural biases, or platform-specific effects from CloudResearch
Incomplete baseline comparisons - no comparison with traditional visualization evaluation methods or heuristic approaches; inter-annotator agreement rates not reported
Limited justification for model selection (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) and no ablation studies on reward function components or their relative contributions
Insufficient statistical rigor - lacks confidence intervals, statistical significance testing, and inter-rater reliability metrics; correlation analysis lacks significance tests
Limited discussion of scalability and maintenance - no clear strategy for extending to other visualization types or updating benchmark as visualization practices evolve
Some technical details unclear - candidate strategy generation for expert review and quality control algorithm mechanisms could be better explained

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous benchmark construction with 3,090 expert-annotated samples across 32 chart types, featuring a systematic three-stage annotation workflow with quality control and expert adjudication
Well-motivated evaluation framework grounded in classical visualization design theory (Fidelity, Expressiveness, Aesthetics) with clear operationalization into six orthogonal sub-dimensions

Extensive experimental evaluation of 12 representative MLLMs with detailed analysis of systematic biases, score distributions, case studies, and real-world applications demonstrating methodological thoroughness
Strong reproducibility commitment with detailed appendices documenting hyperparameters, prompts, evaluation criteria, and plan to release benchmark data and model weights
Practical validation through integration into real-world systems (MatPlotAgent, HAIChart) showing applicability beyond the benchmark itself
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—core contribution is dataset creation combined with standard LoRA fine-tuning on existing models; no novel architectures, training paradigms, or algorithmic innovations

Ground truth reliability concerns: human inter-rater agreement shows low MAE (0.64-0.70) for 1-5 scale, especially for aesthetic dimensions acknowledged as culturally subjective; 88.7% US annotators introduce cultural bias in aesthetic preferences

Modest absolute performance despite statistical significance: VisJudge achieves 0.687 correlation with human ratings (low human baseline of 0.428 suggests task ambiguity); real-world improvements are incremental (+6.07 for MatPlotAgent)

Weak inter-rater agreement (0.428 correlation) suggests the framework's ground truth is inherently ambiguous, particularly for aesthetic assessment; paper acknowledges design style classification is 'coarse-grained and subjective' yet doesn't adequately address implications

Limited analytical insights: paper documents that MLLMs struggle with visualization assessment (unsurprising) but provides minimal explanation of why or actionable insights for improvement; systematic analysis of failure modes by dimension, complexity, or chart type is absent

Dataset scope limitations: static visualizations only (acknowledged lack of dynamic/interactive content), web-crawled with unknown selection bias, heavily chart-focused without coverage of scientific visualizations or geospatial data

Insufficient statistical rigor: no confidence intervals or significance tests reported; test set of only 648 samples (20%) may be insufficient; no ablation on framework design choices (1-5 scale, six dimensions)

Overstated claims: 'comprehensive benchmark' is misleading given visualization type limitations; 'first comprehensive benchmark' ignores related work (ViEval, VIS-Shepherd); claims about 'closing gap with human judgment' unsupported by modest correlations

Evaluation methodology concerns: strong 'evaluation personalities' across models (Figure 5) suggest learning of biased patterns rather than genuine quality understanding; paper acknowledges but doesn't adequately address implications for model quality

Important limitations scattered throughout or relegated to appendices (cultural bias, weak inter-rater agreement) rather than prominently discussed in main text; ethics statement (one paragraph) inadequately addresses encoding aesthetic preferences

strengths: Novel and well-motivated contribution addressing a clear gap in evaluating MLLMs' visualization assessment capabilities
Rigorous dataset construction with 3,090 professionally annotated samples using three-stage annotation workflow with comprehensive quality control
Well-grounded evaluation framework (Fidelity-Expressiveness-Aesthetics) operationalized into six measurable sub-dimensions with clear scoring rubrics
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 12 representative MLLMs with detailed analysis of model-specific biases and capabilities
Strong practical results: VisJudge achieves 23.9% MAE reduction and 60.5% correlation improvement over best general MLLM (GPT-5)
Methodological rigor with multi-layered quality control including validation checks, conflict resolution, and expert review
Excellent reproducibility support with detailed appendices, hyperparameter settings, and commitment to release benchmark and trained models
Generalization validated on two real-world applications (MaiPlotAgent, HAIChart) demonstrating practical utility beyond benchmark
weaknesses: Limited coverage of dynamic and interactive visualizations; dataset primarily static with temporal evolution and interactivity not deeply explored

Generalization concerns: data primarily from web sources with inherent bias, limited domain-specific generalization tests beyond two applications, primarily English-speaking annotators may introduce cultural bias in aesthetic judgments

Evaluation framework validation incomplete: subjective aspects (especially aesthetics) could be more thoroughly validated, limited ablation studies on framework design choices, design style classification relatively coarse-grained
Model fine-tuning scope limited to Qwen2.5-VL-7B variants; claims of broad applicability would be strengthened by fine-tuning on more diverse architectures
Statistical analysis lacks formal significance testing for claimed improvements; no confidence intervals or uncertainty quantification reported
Systematic error analysis by visualization type and dimension incomplete; limited guidance on which types are consistently challenging and why
Computational efficiency not addressed: no discussion of inference time, model size, or resource requirements for practical deployment
Annotation disagreement patterns by visualization type and dimension not thoroughly analyzed, potentially missing insights into framework clarity
